Disposed
dĭ-spōzd'
adj. and v. (inclined, minded to do a thing; also set in order, arranged by another's hand)
Latin disponere, to place apart, to arrange, from dis-, apart, and ponere, to place. The English keeps both senses: a man disposed to go, and a world disposed by God.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The word runs in two directions in the Authorized Version and the two together make a doctrine. Of men it means inclination: Apollos, “when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace” (Act 18:27). Paul uses it of an ordinary decision about a supper: “If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake” (1Co 10:27) — a Christian may accept an unbeliever's invitation, and the conscience is not to be tortured over the meat. Of God the word means arrangement: Elihu asks, “Dost thou know when God disposed them, and caused the light of his cloud to shine?” (Job 37:15). Proverbs joins the two senses in one sentence about a man and a lot: the disposing is the LORD's. So Scripture allows a believer real inclination, real liberty, and real choice, and at the same time asserts that the ordering of all things belongs to God — and Acts 18 shows both at once, a man disposed to travel and a church helped much through grace by his arrival.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) gives to dispose as to set in order, to arrange, to distribute; and, in the passive, to be inclined or minded — the mind bent toward a thing.

expand to see more

DISPOSE, v.t. [L. dispono; dis and pono, to set, place.] To set; to place or distribute; to arrange.

2. To regulate; to adjust; to set in right order.

3. To apply to a particular purpose; to give; to bestow.

DISPOSED, pp. Set in order; arranged; placed; adjusted; inclined; minded. Ye be disposed to go. 1 Cor. x.

Key Scripture

Act 18:27 — "And when he was disposed to pass into Achaia, the brethren wrote, exhorting the disciples to receive him: who, when he was come, helped them much which had believed through grace:"

1Co 10:27 — "If any of them that believe not bid you to a feast, and ye be disposed to go; whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake."

Job 37:15 — "Dost thou know when God disposed them, and caused the light of his cloud to shine?"

Pro 16:9 — "A man's heart deviseth his way: but the LORD directeth his steps."

Modern Corruption

Christian liberty is either abolished by scruple or stretched into license, while 1 Corinthians 10:27 gives a plain rule that does neither.

expand to see more

Paul's instruction about the unbeliever's table is remarkably free, and both the strict and the loose have trouble with it. If ye be disposed to go — the apostle does not command attendance and does not forbid it; the inclination is left with the Christian. Whatsoever is set before you, eat, asking no question for conscience sake — the believer is not to conduct an inquiry into the provenance of the meat. That single rule cuts through an enormous amount of manufactured scruple, in which a Christian is made to examine the associations of every ordinary thing until he cannot eat a meal in peace. The context does not leave him without limits: the very next verse says that if a man tells him the meat was offered in sacrifice, he is to refrain, for the other man's conscience. Liberty is real, and it is governed by love rather than by a list.

The other half of the word supplies the deeper comfort. Elihu's question — dost thou know when God disposed them — puts the arranging of the clouds where the arranging of everything else belongs. A Christian is genuinely disposed to travel, to work, to marry, to accept an invitation; his inclinations are his own and he answers for them. And the same Scripture says the disposing is God's. Reformed doctrine has never resolved this by taking something away from either side, and Acts 18:27 is a small perfect example: Apollos was disposed to go to Achaia, brethren wrote letters, and the result is described as helping much those who had believed through grace. The man's inclination, the church's recommendation, and the sovereign grace of God appear in one sentence without any of the three being reduced.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek boulomai (G1014), to be minded or willing, rendered disposed in Acts 18:27 and 1 Corinthians 10:27; Hebrew sum (H7760), to set or place, of God's ordering in Job.

expand to see more

Greek boulomai (G1014) — to be minded, to purpose; when he was disposed to pass into Achaia; Acts 18:27, 1 Corinthians 10:27.

Greek thelo (G2309) — to will, to desire; the companion verb of inclination throughout the New Testament; Philippians 2:13.

Hebrew sum (H7760) — to put, set, appoint; used of God's ordering of the clouds and the light; Job 37:15.

Hebrew kun (H3559) — to establish, to direct; the LORD directeth the steps of the man who devised his way; Proverbs 16:9.

Greek charis (G5485) — grace; those at Corinth had believed through grace, and were then helped much; Acts 18:27.

Usage

"“When he was disposed to pass into Achaia” — a real inclination, and grace behind the result."

"“If… ye be disposed to go… asking no question for conscience sake” — liberty with a plain rule."

"“When God disposed them” — the same word, and the arranging is His."
